assessment: Nozaki et al. list Parkinson dysphagia, nutrition and complications. The identical title and ten authors recur in 3(2), so count the pair as one probable presentation. The same hospital's related 1999 journal study has an author abstract but does not confirm the proceeding's cohort or name an ingredient.

Identical title and ten authors to the 1999 supplement p. 85, with a different printed page range. The linked abstract is membership-gated. Treat as a probable duplicate listing and do not attribute the related journal study's results to this record.

Toneyama capsaicin jelly presentation names feeding and swallowing disorders. The linked abstract is membership-gated. The public same-year JARM capsaicin-jelly cohort included five Parkinson patients among nine and has a different author list. Overlap and the JSDR sample's diagnosis and outcomes are unknown.

Ichihara et al. compare ALS and Parkinson dysphagia. The linked abstract is membership-gated. Ichihara's later description of institutional coffee-jelly and Calpis contrast boluses does not identify boluses or outcomes from this comparison.

Yoshiura et al. list swallowing therapy for recurrent aspiration pneumonia in young-onset Parkinson disease. Distinct from the Ichihara entry on the same page. The abstract is membership-gated, and no named food, intervention details or case-level outcome were independently found.

Nakata's title attributes return to oral intake in one case to ice massage using chili-treated ponzu ice. It describes a massage exposure, and the public listing leaves diagnosis, ingestion, timing and measured endpoint unresolved. The abstract is membership-gated. The case cannot establish a Parkinson dietary effect.

Ichihara et al. compare stroke, Parkinson disease and ALS swallowing. The authors' 2005 ALS surgery paper cites the original title and page but does not reproduce Parkinson methods or results. The original linked abstract is membership-gated.
A thickened catechin green tea was named for older adults with dysphagia. Member login blocks the methods and results. Parkinson status, formula and comparison are open.

Ito et al. explicitly name cerebrovascular disease in their capsaicin and swallowing title. The original linked abstract is membership-gated, leaving preparation, administration and outcomes unavailable. The public record identifies no Parkinson cohort.

Wakabayashi, Nakagawa and Tsukui report feeding and swallowing rehabilitation in late parkinsonism. The institutional bibliography corroborates the 2004 Niigata meeting. The original linked abstract is membership-gated, leaving subtype, boluses and results unknown.

Musha et al. describe capsaicin in severe dysphagia from a caregiver perspective. The title and shared Midori Hospital authors suggest a linked project with the next abstract. Diagnoses, preparation, route and results are unavailable behind member access.

Doi et al. describe the videofluoroscopy component of a potentially shared Midori Hospital capsaicin project. Exact cohort overlap with the caregiver report is unconfirmed. Member access is required for the original abstract, and the title establishes no Parkinson subgroup, administration or outcomes.

Matsuo et al. part 1 names Parkinson disease and food form effects on feeding and swallowing. Public TOC gives neither named foods nor estimates. Possible 2004 DRS predecessor has a gated collective volume. Saitoh's overlapping author paper used 15 healthy subjects and cannot supply the missing PD results.

Yamamoto et al. part 2 on feeding and swallowing correlation with PD severity is paired with Matsuo's food-form presentation. The TOC supplies no bolus, participants, correlation or sample overlap. No independent outcome established.

Miura et al. capsaicin and swallowing-related apnea duration and breathing pattern. Population, exposure form and result are unknown. Exact title, authors and academic searches uncovered no publicly readable counterpart. Constituent lead for 0724 only.

Yaji et al. reported one Pearl Land Hospital Parkinson patient with disproportionately severe dysphagia relative to physical function. No food, case details or public counterpart located by title and authors.

Mizuno and Oki's title reports improved oral bolus transport when candy and dried squid were used adjunctively at meals in one PD case. Separate effects, dose, outcome methods and aspiration status unresolved. Kakeyu Hospital and author searches did not locate public full abstract. Foods outside the freeze.
The kale alias ケール is part of スケール, a transliteration of scale. The title concerns swallowing assessment and a cognitive scale. No food is named.

Yamamoto et al. parkinsonism aspiration study title names VF but gives no bolus, subgroup or results. A possible overlapping 2010 National Center study reports aspiration in 15/90 idiopathic Parkinson and 16/45 Lewy body dementia participants using liquid VF. The 2006 cohort link and clinical methods remain unconfirmed.

Nagano and Harada describe three progressive supranuclear palsy videofluoroscopy cases. No food or idiopathic Parkinson group in the title. A contemporaneous catheter-nutrition paper by overlapping authors addresses a distinct cohort question. No verified public exact full report.
The short shrimp alias エビ is the start of エビデンス, meaning evidence. The title concerns a nationwide survey in hospitals. No shrimp exposure.

Otaki et al. videofluoroscopy analysis concerns multiple system atrophy. Institutional bibliographies identify contemporaneous and 2008 same-team MSA abstracts. Title gives no foods or idiopathic Parkinson subgroup. No public original results recovered.

Ishida et al. tested the ORA LIGHT oral rehabilitation instrument in a Parkinson case. Title gives no food or clinical effect. Overlapping team also presented a 2006 neuromuscular-disease instrument report without diagnostic confirmation. Case overlap with the 2007 metronome presentation is unconfirmed.

Shibata et al. describe oral dysfunction in MSA. Niigata University confirms the 2007 presentation and lists a same-title 2008 version. Neither public record identifies a PD group, named food or a food outcome.

The conference title names water, milk and palatal muscle activity. The related 2009 full paper tested ten healthy adults, with lower normalized muscle activity after milk. No Parkinson group or clinical aspiration endpoint.

Umemoto et al. compared chewing and swallowing in Parkinson disease and motor neuron disease. Fukuoka University confirms the presentation. The title gives no bolus or result. Related 2008 Yamano study used iopamidol in 16 PD cases, with a different question and unconfirmed cohort overlap.

Matching 2008 Sugishita paper documents 3 mL 50% juice and 1.6% gelatin jelly in one stage III PD case. Juice aspirated at baseline and still penetrated after rhythm therapy despite no aspiration then. Jelly aspirated after indirect therapy, not at baseline or after rhythm. The oral-transit contrast is between rehabilitation phases, with 0.92 s table versus 0.94 s abstract for jelly after rhythm. No named fruit or isolated frozen exposure.

Kobayashi's title reports inhaled black pepper oil in two children. Munakata's overlapping 2008 journal team reported increased oral intake in five of eight children with neurological disorders and tube feeding. No Parkinson subgroup. Participant overlap unverified.

Umemoto title names jaw–tongue coordination and Parkinson dysphagia. A later overlapping team examined 30 Parkinson patients with a single 5 mL barium gelatin jelly. Conference preparation and cohort overlap unverified.
Takai et al. describe swallowing change after deep brain stimulation in one Parkinson patient. The title identifies no food or bolus. Investigator group differs from Kitashima's published series.
Nishi et al. describe dysphagia rehabilitation in one person with progressive supranuclear palsy. The public title gives no preparation or outcome estimate.
The title names Caspian Sea yogurt and endoscopic swallowing assessment. No public body, outcomes or Parkinson cohort verified.
The title names a swallowing and feeding intervention for someone with intellectual disability and Parkinson disease. The bolus, treatment and result remain inaccessible.
The title names a patient with parkinsonism who underwent cricopharyngeal myectomy and laryngeal elevation. The surgical outcome, food preparation and exact diagnosis are unverified.

Maki et al. title identifies three Parkinson cases with discrepant swallowing and motor impairment. No food appears in the title. Later same-institution talks with overlapping authors cannot establish the cohort.

Shibata et al. examine oral function in multiple system atrophy. Niigata profile and later JST bibliographic record identify the same diagnosis, without an idiopathic Parkinson or named food comparison.
Ohtaki et al. describe hospital patients with multiple system atrophy and swallowing impairment. The public title gives no test bolus or Parkinson subgroup.

Shinjo and Yamamoto's questionnaire title has a likely related 2012 publication from the same author group. An author summary names swallowing-screen questions for pills and meal timing rather than a comparative food intervention. Conference sample and questions are unverified.
Tanaka et al. describe interfacility and home care in one person with multiple system atrophy. No test food or Parkinson cohort appears in the title.
Kuraoka et al. study how Parkinson patients and caregivers recognize feeding and swallowing difficulty. Public metadata identify no food or symptom estimate.

The translated Pitts title and original six-author roster match PMID 19029430, online in 2008. Ten men completed four weeks of respiratory training with reduced penetration–aspiration scores on a 30 mL thin barium test. Barium is contrast material.
Nozaki's gated multicenter metronome title has a related 2011 abstract reporting shortened transit and reduced residue with an unidentified jelly in 20 Parkinson patients. Cohort identity unverified.
Yamawaki's thematic presentation covers mechanisms, treatment and rehabilitation of Parkinson dysphagia. The title gives no food or participant results.
Yamamoto's thematic title concerns videofluoroscopy in Parkinson dysphagia. No bolus is named. Later same-author clinical studies do not establish the talk's contents.
Nozaki's thematic presentation concerns approaches to Parkinson swallowing impairment. The title gives no evidence that this talk studied a food or constituent.
Baked banana is a preparation in this dysphagia food-development title. Author listing verified. The body, diagnosis, exact preparation and clinical outcomes are unverified.

Sasaki et al. presented Parkinson dysphagia. The university record confirms the 2009 presentation, and a 2010 TOC has the same title and overlapping author group. Preparation, results and sample overlap remain unverified.
Sugishita et al. compare swallowing kinematics with stimulation on and off. Different authors from Kitashima's DBS series. The bolus and results remain unverified.

Kitashima's title on chewing and swallowing after DBS leads to a 2010 talk and a 2011 primary three-case paper. The paper used barium with commercial thickener adjusted to honey-like viscosity. Conference and paper participant overlap unverified.
Kawamichi et al. title specifies a clavicle-band posture intervention in a Parkinson case with neck flexion. Gated body leaves swallowing preparation and result unverified.

Han et al. title describes an association between depression and dysphagia independent of motor severity. Related 2010 and 2011 journal reports concern questionnaire associations. The accessible 2011 abstract has n=127 and no food exposure.
The shrimp alias 海老 appears in the hospital name 海老名, Ebina. The title describes hospital swallowing service statistics. No food is named.
The kale alias ケール is part of スケール, a transliteration of scale. The title concerns post-stroke prognostication. No food is named.

Yamagiwa et al. title reports improved fluid intake in three people with severe motor and intellectual disabilities after black pepper oil use. No Parkinson diagnosis, route, ingredient details or swallowing outcome verified.
Nishida et al. title concerns factors affecting oral intake in Parkinson. Public metadata identify no foods, factors or estimates. A later same-author QoL paper has a different study question.
Mochizuki et al. describe three cases of severe dysphagia in multiple system atrophy. No Parkinson cohort or preparation appears in the title.
Tanaka et al. title describes home diet-texture counseling and quality of life in one person with multiple system atrophy. No named ingredient or idiopathic Parkinson case.
Sato et al. title describes multidisciplinary nutrition and dysphagia rehabilitation in multiple system atrophy. The title has no named food or Parkinson cohort.
The peach alias ピーチ is embedded in the loanword スピーチ, speech. The title concerns cannula changes and swallowing in two tracheostomy cases. No peach is named.
Yamane and Konishi report home rehabilitation and resumption of oral intake in one person with multiple system atrophy. No test food or Parkinson cohort appears in the title.
A green tea thickener guide is the named topic. A university bibliography verifies the series. The title supplies no Parkinson group or outcome.
The shrimp alias 海老 appears in the hospital name 海老名, Ebina. The title describes a regional nutrition and swallowing service case. No food is named.
Mineta et al. title links respiratory and swallowing function in Parkinson. The public TOC does not name a bolus or estimate. Troche's same-issue English-language study is independent.

Kitashima's overlapping 2011 three-case study reports heterogeneous responses to subthalamic stimulation using contrast thickened to honey-like viscosity. Exact 2009 and 2010 presentation participants unverified.
Sasaki et al. title repeats their 2009 Parkinson dysphagia title with overlapping authors. Neither gated body was available to establish sample overlap or bolus.

Ebihara et al. title reports capsiate and swallowing reflex in aspiration pneumonia, also listed at a 2010 rehabilitation meeting. A government grant annex reproduces the earlier randomized letter with reduced swallow latency in 12 older patients receiving CH-19 Sweet capsiate extract in a pharyngeal catheter challenge. Participant overlap unverified. The letter and subsequent seasoning grant do not report a Parkinson subgroup.
Sato et al. title names upper esophageal liquid transit in Parkinson. NCNP ethics record 21-10-事 2 corroborates the study topic and Yamamoto. Composition and findings remain inaccessible.
The title names yogurt and jelly and compares test methods and posture in healthy volunteers. The effect estimates and detailed preparations are unverified.
Nakahashi's title describes resuming home oral intake after gastrostomy in one case of parkinsonism. Etiology, food preparation and swallow outcomes are unverified.
Sasamura et al. title names maximal tongue pressure in Parkinson and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. It gives no food stimulus or results.

The bilingual Troche title and original five-author list match PMID 20623304. Thirty-nine people with Parkinson swallowed thin barium, and higher penetration–aspiration scores corresponded to shorter swallowing apnea and more post-swallow inspiration.
